issues.text: Whether the suspension of pronouncement of the judgment in respect of the police officer was compatible with the obligation to protect the right to life by law within the meaning of Article 2 of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: The applicants alleged that their relative had been deliberately killed by a police officer in breach of Article 2 of the Convention. They complained that the suspension of pronouncement of the judgment in respect of the police officer was not compatible with the obligation to protect the right to life by law within the meaning of Article 2 of the Convention.

issues.text: Whether there had been serious shortcomings in the investigation into the shooting and in the trial of the police officer

anchor.surface_text: Relying on Articles 2 and 13 of the Convention, the applicants also complained that there had been serious shortcomings in the investigation into the shooting and in the trial of the police officer.

issues.text: Whether the national authorities afforded appropriate and sufficient redress for the violation of Article 2

anchor.surface_text: The Court’s examination of the applicants’ complaint will therefore be limited to ascertaining whether or not the national authorities afforded appropriate and sufficient redress for the violation (see Fadime and Turan Karabulut v. Turkey, no. 23872/04, § 43, 27 May 2010 and Külah and Koyuncu v. Turkey, no. 24827/05, § 38, 23 April 2013) and whether they have complied with their substantive and procedural obligations under Article 2 of the Convention.

Turkey, no. 24827/05, § 38, 23 April 2013) and whether they have complied with their substantive and procedural obligations under Article 2 of the Convention.

issues.text: Whether the application is admissible under Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: The Court notes that the admissibility rules are set out in Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention. It considers that submitting a summary of the information provided on the application form does not constitute an admissibility criterion as laid down in these Articles. Therefore, the Government’s objection must consequently be dismissed.

issues.text: Whether the trial court’s decision to suspend the pronouncement of the judgment under Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure results in impunity and undermines deterrence

anchor.surface_text: The Court notes that the suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment, regulated by Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, results in the impunity of the perpetrators. That is because the application of this provision deprives the judgment of all its legal consequences, including the sentence, provided that the offender abides by the supervision order.

issues.text: Whether the national courts exercised their discretion to minimise the consequences of an unlawful act rather than showing that such acts could in no way be tolerated

anchor.surface_text: The Court therefore considers that the impugned court decision suggests that the judges exercised their discretion to minimise the consequences of an unlawful act, rather than showing that such acts could in no way be tolerated (see mutatis mutandis, Eski v. Turkey, no. 8354/04, § 36, 5 June 2012).

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court relied on the domestic court's findings to establish a breach of Article 2.

arguments.claim: The State’s positive obligation under Article 2 requires the domestic legal system to enforce criminal law against those unlawfully taking life.

anchor.surface_text: The Court reiterates that the State’s positive obligation under Article 2 of the Convention to protect life by law requires the domestic legal system to demonstrate its capacity to enforce the criminal law against those who have unlawfully taken the life of another...

arguments.claim: National courts should not allow life-endangering offences, including negligence leading to death, to go unpunished to maintain public confidence and rule of law.

anchor.surface_text: It must be emphasised that, although there is no absolute obligation for all prosecutions to result in conviction or in a particular sentence, the national courts should not under any circumstances be prepared to allow life-endangering offences, including those arising from the negligence of agents that leads to a death, to go unpunished. This is essential for maintaining public confidence, ensuring adherence to the rule of law and preventing any appearance of tolerance of or collusion in unlawful acts...

arguments.claim: The Court grants substantial deference to national courts in choice of sanctions but intervenes in cases of manifest disproportion between gravity of act and punishment imposed.

anchor.surface_text: Although the Court should grant substantial deference to the national courts in the choice of appropriate sanctions for ill-treatment and homicide by State agents, it must exercise a certain power of review and intervene in cases of manifest disproportion between the gravity of the act and the punishment imposed...

arguments.claim: The trial court found the police officer guilty of causing death by negligence but suspended the pronouncement of the judgment, lessening consequences of a serious criminal act rather than showing intolerance.

anchor.surface_text: In the present case, the Court reiterates that the trial court found the police officer guilty for causing the death of the applicants’ relative by negligence... However, the Court observes that the domestic law permitted the trial court to suspend the pronouncement of the judgment for the offence of unlawful killing. By this decision, the trial court used its power of discretion to lessen the consequences of a serious criminal act rather than to show that such acts could in no way be tolerated...

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that suspension of judgment resulted in impunity and undermined deterrence, thus rejecting the adequacy of the sanction.

arguments.claim: Suspension of pronouncement of judgment under Article 231 results in impunity as it deprives the judgment of all legal consequences if offender abides by supervision order.

anchor.surface_text: The Court notes that the suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment, regulated by Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, results in the impunity of the perpetrators. That is because the application of this provision deprives the judgment of all its legal consequences, including the sentence, provided that the offender abides by the supervision order.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that this legal provision leads to impunity and undermines the deterrent effect required by Article 2.

arguments.claim: The impugned court decision suggests judges exercised discretion to minimise consequences of unlawful act rather than showing such acts could not be tolerated.

anchor.surface_text: The Court therefore considers that the impugned court decision suggests that the judges exercised their discretion to minimise the consequences of an unlawful act, rather than showing that such acts could in no way be tolerated...

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court rejected the adequacy of the judicial response as it failed to demonstrate intolerance of unlawful acts.

arguments.claim: The criminal-law system as applied to the killing of Murat Kasap was far from rigorous and had little deterrent effect to prevent unlawful acts.

anchor.surface_text: In conclusion, the Court considers that the criminal-law system, as applied to the killing of Murat Kasap, proved to be far from rigorous and had little deterrent effect capable of ensuring the effective prevention of unlawful acts, such as those complained of by the applicants.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the system inadequate to fulfill Article 2 positive obligations and ensure deterrence.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT UNANIMOUSLY

1.  Declares the application admissible;
2.  Holds that there has been a violation of Article 2 of the Convention;

3.  Holds

(a)  that the respondent State is to pay, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, EUR 30,000 (thirty thousand euros) to the first applicant and EUR 10,000 (ten thousand euros) jointly to the other applicants, plus any tax that may be chargeable, in respect of non-pecuniary damage, to be converted into the national currency of the respondent State at the rate applicable at the date of settlement;

(b)  that from the expiry of the above-mentioned three months until settlement simple interest shall be payable on the above amount at a rate equal to the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank during the default period plus three percentage points;
4.  Dismisses the remainder of the applicants’ claim for just satisfaction.

edges.explanation: The issue whether there had been serious shortcomings in the investigation and trial addresses the concept of Article 13 effective remedy as applicants complained relying on Articles 2 and 13.
Issue i3 addresses whether national authorities afforded appropriate redress for violation of Article 2, requiring the positive obligations doctrine c4.
Issue i4 concerns whether national authorities complied with substantive and procedural obligations under Article 2, which is the positive obligation doctrine c4.
Issue i7 concerns whether courts minimized consequences of unlawful acts rather than showing intolerance, which relates to the positive obligations doctrine c4.
The issue whether national courts exercised discretion relates to the doctrine essence of the right as noted by the Court.
